visible.summary: Direction: better than the national position - the oldest and deepest regional framework in Spain. Ley 2/2014, an integral law for non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity, was among the first trans-specific regional laws in Europe; Ley 8/2017 of 28 December (in force 4 February 2018) guarantees LGTBI rights and equal treatment for LGTBI people and their families; and the regional government approved an equality strategy for 2024-2028 on 26 December 2024. Visitor-relevant geography: Andalucía carries much of Spain's LGBTQ mass tourism (Mijas, Torremolinos, Seville), which coexists with school-content opt-out ('pin parental') conflicts that historically concentrated in Andalusian municipalities.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 'pin parental' school-content conflicts that historically concentrated in Andalusian municipalities are an LGTBI-visibility issue rather than trans-specific, but they mark the civic climate a visibly queer visitor reads locally.

sources.claim: State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the national 'Trans Law' for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of LGBTI rights, applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, including this one: adults may rectify the registered sex entry without prior surgical reassignment, the right to the registered change being grounded in the free development of personality (art. 10.1 CE). The law further defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the causes covered, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances - the national framework the regional position in this record rests on.

Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) on the Spanish Congress's passage of the national Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment requirements; children from age 12 may obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. The law also strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples and combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. These are the national provisions this autonomous community implements under the same framework.

visible.summary: No voivodeship-level trans-specific resolution, incident series or enforcement finding was located for this division in the current research pass. The anti-LGBT municipal-resolution wave (80+ municipalities and four voivodeship-level declarations as of March 2020) concentrated in the eastern and south-eastern parts of the country, so the absence of local findings here indicates thinner documentation rather than established safety. The national frame governs this division: no hate-crime protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds (the March 2025 amendment bill referred to the Constitutional Tribunal, hearings held July and September 2025), court-based and medically gatekept legal gender recognition, and national sources documenting a trans foreign woman held in a male-only guarded detention centre and an ECtHR ruling that denying a prisoner hormone therapy violates private life.
visible.tangentialFactors: The national criminal-code amendment that would have added sexual-orientation and gender-identity hate-crime grounds remains suspended at the constitutional court, so all offences here are prosecuted without SOGI aggravation; the nationwide anti-LGBT municipal-declaration wave (80+ municipalities, concentrated in other voivodeships) shapes the surrounding climate even without a declaration in this division.
visible.localsOnly: The court-based, medically gatekept legal-gender-recognition regime is resident-facing; the ECtHR hormone-therapy ruling concerned a resident prisoner, and prison health provisions bind the state for residents and pre-trial detainees alike.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Passport theft, overcharging by unlicensed taxis, and general urban crime affect all travellers here and are not trans-specific.

sources.claim: Association for Legal Intervention (13 Mar 2024): a Polish regional court placed a transgender woman (Vietnamese citizen, on hormone therapy since 2018) in a guarded centre for male foreigners; Border Guard refused to move/release her despite her identifying as a woman and warning that stopping medication would harm her. After an intervention by the legal-aid organisation citing Polish law, court rulings and international standards, the Border Guard Commander released her because continued detention there posed a serious health risk. Useful to this record: in Poland, detained foreign trans women face placement in male-only facilities until formally challenged, and release can depend on legal intervention.

TGEU, 16 Jul 2024: on 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) found Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 (right to private and family life) of the ECHR by denying a trans woman access to hormone replacement therapy while imprisoned, despite her having been prescribed hormones for almost two years; the Court awarded EUR 8,000 damages. Useful to this record: a trans visitor who is detained in Poland has a Europe-wide human-rights remedy against denial of HRT, though enforcement required litigation.

visible.summary: No state-specific trans-related source was found for this division in the current research pass: no local incident series and no documented enforcement divergence from the national frame. The national law applies here in full — the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (up to 14 years, extends to tourists, bans LGBTQ+ organisations and public expression of identity) plus the inherited criminal provisions; national monitoring recorded 89 extortions, 118 harassment incidents and more than 20 unlawful detentions of LGBTQ+ people by law-enforcement officials in 2024 alone, with detentions for "looking gay" and release on payment of a bribe reported. This division sits outside the twelve northern states that carry a separate religious-law death-penalty regime for same-sex conduct. Dating-app "kito" extortion gangs are a nationwide app-user risk, and foreign government travel advice warns LGBT travellers of arrest, violence and blackmail.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2014 Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act (up to 14 years, applies to tourists, bans LGBTQ+ organisations and public expression) shapes police and prosecutorial posture toward anyone perceived as same-sex-active, including gender-nonconforming visitors, everywhere in this country including this division; dating-app "kito" extortion gangs present a documented app-user risk to gay and trans people alike. The separate religious-law death-penalty regime for same-sex conduct applies only in the twelve northern states, not in this division.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Armed insurgency in the north-east (Boko Haram), kidnapping, and violent crime affect travellers in many parts of the country; these are general hazards, not trans-specific.

sources.claim: Report (August 2026) on the latest UK travel advice for this country: warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation; up to 14 years for same-sex sexual activity; some northern states' religious law can prescribe the death penalty; the 2014 Act also punishes assisting, attending or promoting same-sex relationships and LGBTQ+ organisations; separately warns of short-notice curfews and vehicle-movement restrictions, mobile-network shutdowns with little notice, and political rallies and communal violence.

The national-framework page under which a visitor to Cross River stands: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 makes same-sex marriage or civil union, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or publicly showing same-sex affection, punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide, and the Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men (14 years) and gross indecency between men (3 years). The twelve northern states under Shari'a law — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — carry up to a death-penalty maximum, and Cross River is not among them, matching the record's claim. The page documents the nationwide 'kito' entrapment-and-blackmail scheme targeting gay men and trans women, police profiling and extortion of people perceived as gay, and mass arrests (42 men in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri, August 2023; 76 in Gombe, October 2023), with no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Confirms every national-framework element the record asserts for this state: the 14-year ceiling, exclusion from the sharia death-penalty regime, kito/gang risk and enforcement pattern.

Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents the abuse pattern this record attributes to law enforcement: arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion using threats and acts of physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. Research was conducted in June and July 2010 in Lagos, Anambra and Kaduna states and the federal capital as case studies of three of Nigeria's six geopolitical zones; the report is national in scope and does not name Cross River. It substantiates the record's national baseline that police treat suspected same-sex conduct and perceived 'gayness' as an extortion opportunity, with release on payment of a bribe as the documented outcome.
